And the bald spot on his whole i bead shines. "Well," thinks Taira," now I'll not miss him; goand stand at tha door. Them we sha'n't miss each other." Yelim went and stood and stood, lie stood there half the day : all the people went out —.02, bum spent six woeks in Jerusalem. and visited every thing; MA in Bethlehem, and Bethany, and on the Jordan : awl lie had a seal stamped on a .w shirt at the Lord's sepulchre. no that he might be buried in it; and lie got some Jordan water in a vial, and some earth; and lie got some candles with the holy lire, and he noted down his recollections ! in all places; and having swat all his money, except enough to get him home, Yefim started on his home- journey. Ile went to Jaffa, took passage in a ship, sailed to Odessa, and started to walk home. XI. Yefim walks alone over the same road as before. As he began to near his home, again the worriment came spoil him as to hew the folks were getting along without him. "In a year,' thinks he," meek water leaks away. You spend a whole lifetime making a house and it don't take long to go to waste." flow his son -conducted affairs? how had the spring ommed up? how had the cattle weathered the winter? how had they done the Wei ? Yefim reached that place where, the year before, lie had parted from Yells& It was impossible to recognize the people. Where, the preceding year, the people were wretchedly poor, non, all lived in sufficient comfort. There had been good crops. The people had recovered, and forgotten their former trouble. Venni at evening reached the very village where, the year before. Yelisk had stopped. Ile had hardly entered the village, when a little girl in a white shirt sprang out from behind a hut Grandpa 7 Dear grandpa! Come into our house! Yellin was inclined to go on, but the little girl would not allow him: she seizes him by the skirts, pulls him along into the hut, and laughs. There came out upon the doorsteps a Woman with a little boy ; she alna beckons to him: "Come in, please, grand-sire, er p'delhho, -and take supper with us, --you shall spend the night." The Cunard Royal Mail steamer Servia, which i arrived on Monday morning from New York, brings particulars af the loss of the Newcastle steamer Earinnoor in the West Indies, with nineteen of her crow, while on a voyage from Baltimore to Rio Janeiro, talon with wheat. On the 4th of Septem- ber the Femme, encountered a hurricane, and the steamer woo hove to for several hours. She wee very heavily laden, and was no deep in the water that the seas made a clean sweep over her decks for boars. The Earnmoor', triple-expansion engines, of 250-horse power, were unable to keep her head to the storm and she broached to. The sea 11110,11h1 the fire seen and extinguished the fires, leaving the vessel wholly at the memy of the gale. During part of the night the crew worked at the pumps in a last effort to save the ship, but the frightful pomading which the hull continued to receive by the mountainous waves caused the seams to open, and the water poured in from below and above, and wined to rapidly en the wearied men that it did not take long to mein, the hopelessness of the task. As near as it could be told by dead reekoning,the Earnmoor was then about 350 miles off the lower coed of Florida,and not very far east of the 1 Bahama Islands. Captain Gray finally gave up hope, ' and ordered the boats tette lowered on the morning of the sth of September. Water and provisiens worn taken on board, and the crew put off from the sinking vessel in the midst of the raging storm. The captain, with his chief engineer, second mate, and loot the crew, occupied the long boat, while the first mato, second engineer, and five of the crew were in the snmll boat. The force of the hurricane and the shifting winds soon separated the boats, and nothing has since been heard of the captain's boat. There is little doubt that the beat and all M it perished in the cyclone. For over three weeks the first mate and his exhausted crew ,J 5 six in their little yawl kept up the struggle. Day after day 'lamed without the sight eta asti, until hope began to give way to despair. The provisions and water began to run low. First all hands were put On short allowance, whielt had to be nff tics! from day to-lay, until the last bit of biscuit and the last cup of water was gone • and then came a time of suet. suffering as only a man Afflo 11510 hillVielf been shipwrecked can form an idea of. After they had been drifting for twenty-two dAys that last drt•ad altsrnatiye of ship- wrecked men began to force itself into the minds of the famished seamen—who should be the man to lay down his life to save the others from starvation ? The ghastly alternative, imwever, was not resorted to, because on the twenty-thirst day a vessel hove in sight. Only one man in the boat was stntng enough to hold a signal s° as to attract the attention of the craft. She was the nelerate, Mostplito. from New York, bound for Truxillo. She speedily bore down nn the shipx-reeked men, whose dejection Ws, turned to delirious joy when the famished mariners saw that their signals were seen and that they were saved. The starving men were taken aboard the schooner anti landed at Nassau, New Pmvidenee, on the 30th September, snore dntd than alive. The engineer and the seamen were suffering from such extreme phy- sical exhaustion that it sr feared they will die, while the fimt mate had only strength auffichrat to give a vague account of Use disaster.

div.head: CUNARD STEAMER ASHORE.
div.p: A CUNARD STEAMER ASHORE.

The Cunard steamship Malta, while proceeding trots, Liverpool tio Falmouth, is r.,,ter fin the Mediterranean, ran ashore at Cape Cornwall during a dense big abodt nine ocloek on Inisday night. Efforts were at once made to buid the passengers, everyone of whom was gat mfely ashore and landed at Wheal Castle, a niMe a lib's, to the north ft Cape Cornwall. One stoker was tin 'wired wish' geLting into a hoot. The Malta grounffed in a Stack fog right in the %awn, huge chasm in the rafts, north of Wheal Castle. hitter lights were homing, and the sea was perfectly calm. The steamer has since be- come a wreck. The passengers, tiighteen in number, including on ladies, were reteued and sheltered in the cottages of the Cornish miners. On Wednesday, the: crew lanild at Falmouth. The cargo, a valuable 03,3, living dispemed by the heavy swell which breaks ~v•re the wreck.

div.head: TASTE FOR JAN.
div.p: A TASTE FOR JAN.

On Saturday night, a girl named Louisa Corbett, twelve years of age, who lives with her parents in Challinor-st., was in the shop of Charles Parker, i provision dealer. Church-st.. when she yielded to I temptation, and made off with two pits of jam. She was charged with the offence before the magistrates, on Monday, when she was discharged. A convic- tion was, however, recorded against her, and the Bench ordered payment of the value of the stolen goods—lid.

I AN ORPHAN'S ADVENTI.RE. William Henry Bettie a youth, admitted having ! travelled without ticket, from Liverpool to War- rington, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, on the day previous. Ile told the magistrates that he was an orphan. and had been in a Boy's Refuge at Liver- 1: pool. The Bench remanded the case in order that I enquiries might be made as to the correctness of his story. Bethell was again brought up on Thur. I day morning, when it transpired that the statement he had made was correct. On the suggestion of the Chief ConA able, the sem of :!,..141. was allowed out of the Poor 800, in which to pay the lade fare to Manchester, and get him a dinner. The authorities at Alison's Home, Manchester. wrote to the police intimating that Betheli would be re-admitted.

Hart, John Peter Woods, and Ellen Daviea' were I charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-et., at midnight on Saturday. Hart and Woods were charged with having rescued the female prisoner from custody, and Hart, who ia a soldier from Orford barracks, was also charged with having damaged Constable Evans' helmet. Con- stables Evans and 'lampson took the temale prisoner into custody for creating a disturbance, and the male prisoners, after a struggle, r.•seu..d bee. Sir—As yeal stifle titae ago announced to the public that I applied for a summons against the Corporation for creating a nuisance itt the Howley depot, thereby deatroying the health of the people in the neighbour- Imal,just permit me tansy that, in the interval between the application for the summons and the time for action, the authorities of the town sent form. to ask if I would adjourn the summons. ..ring no that they were mak- ing a last effort tat cure the nuisance I complained of, and it would be sueccsrful. Not wishing unnecessarily to harass the Sanitary Committee, I consented to with- draw it, at the sante time declaring that it was money being wasted and the nuisance would not be cured. . . .

I visitol the Howley depot whilst this last experiment was going on. and, although not allowed to go inside by the order of the II rough Surveyor,l found that they were ! carrying large pip,o underground to the large chimney belonging to the Castle Rubber Works by the river shle, intending I. make the use of this chimney to carry off the stench. I wittiest out to the Rubber 'Company the injudiciousness of allowing this—that they themselves were not entirely tree from creating a nuisance, and the two combinol might prove very serious, but added that this new scheme would not succeed. Now, any one with a grain of common-sense shoukl have known that forcing a current of cold air, such as this, would greatly interfere with the usual draft of the chimney. soils-Is proved to be the ease, and had to be shut off. The stink , at times since has beets as bid as ever, and this number eight experiment has failed. What is the I ask, of going on withthee.expensive experiments by parties who are not competent? Why do I notour rope...nation intheCouncil demand a thorough overhauling of the wheaectmcern, even if it should nece. sitate the railing in ef 5555 e firstsiassengineerwhowould report on the whole affair from the ipgitstsisg up to now? It may well be seriously asked what is the use of licoe ing borrowing and spending money upon what every experienced man knows will be a failure ? I still stick to my former statement, toad,- a little while ago, that the pip. through which the excreta is env-sod to Long- ford will silt up, and steps should id 435ee be taken to ascertain whether this is soar not, before the borrowing ef the £7OOO is sanctioned, bee... as I have stated, the silting ttp at these pipes will be fatal lathe whole scheme. sincerely trust that all the oppteitiou that can be will be brought before the Commissioner next week with a view of preventing this money being got. and furtleTing, if possible, the object of removing these nuning dens ot disease from our midst. —Yours truly WILLIAM PIGGLE. div.head: ELOPEMENT OF A NAVVY'S WIFE
div.p: ELOPEMENT OF A NAVVY'S WIFE
FROM RUNCORN.

Five months experience of things matrimonial, has placed Charles Williams.of Cawder-st., Runcorn, in a position to give important testimony on the j question "In marriage a failure.' Williams iso Ship Canal navvy and until recently wan employed at , Weston Point. Almut live months ago at WiaaeN he J took to wife a young woman bearing the quiet j homely name of Martha, and he had no cause to suspect she was unfaithful to him until the 2nd October, when on coming home to his tea, after working from five o'clock in the morning, he found J that she bad departed with a miner named Edward Evans. She had also taken with hrr a silver watch-! china. four knives and forks, six spoons, a table- cloth and other articles. Williams promptly took out a warrant against his .better half' for thiev- ing but nothing was known of the whereabouts of the missing one until Ti.esday, when she wrote asking Williams to forgive her. On Wednesday l'.C. Woodrow proceeded to Cbapel-en-le-Frith, in Derbyshire. and apprehended the wanderer as she was entering the Post Oilier to inquire for a letter. 10 reply to the charge of theft she sail. •• What's Ids is mine." and she had a somewhat similar story to tell the Runcorn magistrates, on Thursday. whe'n she woo brought up for judgment. She had taken the articles, she mkt, because she thought they would be safer with her, as her husband would only make away with them. She also made the interest- ing confession that she would have come back to j Roncorn the day after she left, but she was afraid her husband had gone away. The magistrates J ordered the woman to pay a tine of Rh., or go to gaol for a month's hard labour. She entreated her hu-band to pay the money and have her liberated, but he declined. and said he had been true to her, and she ought to have Well true to him.

BURNS'S LEAP FROif LONDON BRIDGE.

Tommy Burns.whojt will be recollectetthas under- taken to walk from Liverpool to London and back and dive front a bridge at each end of the journey, arrived in London on Monday afternoon. Burns, : began his self-imposed task on Wednesday evening. , when, it is alleged, be dived from Runcorn Brultie. a height of 8.7. feet, and then swain to Liverpool. IS miles away, in the course of four hours. Ills journey in the water over. he set out on his long tramp to London. Quick progress was made, and hy half-past five o'clock on Saturday afternoon North- ampton was reached. 11Pre a halt woo made until Sunday tlyetting, and Bunts again made for London at five minutes past twelve, on that night. Thence his route lay is Queen's Cross, Newport, Woburn, Donstable, St. Allians,and j Whetstone. The Angel at Islington was reached I at three o'clock on Ylonday, mei then he proceeded to London Bridge to make preparations for the next feat. Some time was now wasted. for the police had to be evaded, whilst no little, difficulty was found in procuring a roc •au oa which in go off, con' segue/nen the number of people on the bridge, all lof whom were anxiously watching the heats in a regatta. At her -el, however, Bums saw an oppor- tunny, and quickly divesting himself of ia clothes. Ihe appeared dressed in a neat costume of red. All was now in readiu .s, and. mounting the parapet, he took a header into the st ream. Just before he got to the sinter, however, he appeared to linen a somersault and fall on Ids back. On rising to the I surface he swam nearly a quarter of a tittle befon, getting into the skiff Whiell was in waiting for him. From first to last. no interference was met with from the pahae. Born, started on his return journey I at is quarter to two on Tuesday.
